title: Leg Lock Safety Hierarchy
shortDefinition: The safety order: recognize entanglement, hide heel, protect knee line, clear secondary leg, then exit with control.
whyItMatters: Leg locks can become dangerous quickly if you rotate wrong while knee line is trapped.
deepExplanation: The safety hierarchy prevents panic. Heel exposure is the signal, knee line is the boundary, secondary leg is the extra lock. Early tapping and clear communication are technical skills.
beginnerView: Do not rotate when heel is exposed and knee line is trapped.
advancedView: Read leg entanglements as control positions, not twisting races.

ifThenExamples.if: If you lose Leg Lock Safety Hierarchy during the exchange.
ifThenExamples.then: Stop accelerating, recover the nearest body structure, then continue the technique.
ifThenExamples.why: Modern no-gi punishes forceful continuation after structure is lost.

ifThenExamples.if: If the opponent correctly answers your first line.
ifThenExamples.then: Use Leg Lock Safety Hierarchy to switch to a safer branch instead of forcing the same line.
ifThenExamples.why: A good concept turns the opponent’s reaction into information for the next decision.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Leg Lock Safety Hierarchy is a single technical trick.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: Treat it as a decision rule that appears across many positions.

commonMisunderstandings.misunderstanding: Understanding the concept automatically makes it work live.
commonMisunderstandings.correction: The concept needs body signals, short cues, and positional rolling.

trainingCues: Name Leg Lock Safety Hierarchy before adding force.
Find the body signal instead of guessing generally.
If structure is lost, reset one layer first.
Drill slowly, then test with progressive resistance.
